name: Action Figures
description: There is a shop that sells action figures near Monocarp's house. A new set of action figures will be released shortly; this set contains $$$n$$$ figures, the $$$i$$$-th figure costs $$$i$$$ coins and is available for purchase from day $$$i$$$ to day $$$n$$$. For each of the $$$n$$$ days, Monocarp knows whether he can visit the shop. Every time Monocarp visits the shop, he can buy any number of action figures which are sold in the shop (of course, he cannot buy an action figure that is not yet available for purchase). If Monocarp buys at least two figures during the same day, he gets a discount equal to the cost of the most expensive figure he buys (in other words, he gets the most expensive of the figures he buys for free). Monocarp wants to buy exactly one $$$1$$$-st figure, one $$$2$$$-nd figure, ..., one $$$n$$$-th figure from the set. He cannot buy the same figure twice. What is the minimum amount of money he has to spend?
input_specification: The first line contains one integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 10^4$$$) — the number of test cases. Each test case consists of two lines: the first line contains one integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 4 \cdot 10^5$$$) — the number of figures in the set (and the number of days); the second line contains a string $$$s$$$ ($$$|s| = n$$$, each $$$s_i$$$ is either 0 or 1 ). If Monocarp can visit the shop on the $$$i$$$-th day, then $$$s_i$$$ is 1 ; otherwise, $$$s_i$$$ is 0 . Additional constraints on the input: in each test case, $$$s_n$$$ is 1 , so Monocarp is always able to buy all figures during the $$$n$$$-th day; the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$4 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, print one integer — the minimum amount of money Monocarp has to spend.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 2026C — Action Figures [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
